name: Treaty with the Chippewa of the Mississippi and Lake Superior, 1847 (Treaty of Fond du Lac)
promises: Article 3: $17,000 in specie to the Lake Superior Ojibwe and $17,000 to the Mississippi Ojibwe within six months of ratification, plus $1,000 a year for forty-six years to the Mississippi bands, which they could direct to schools, blacksmiths and laborers.
Article 3: Ojibwe of full or mixed blood to be employed as teachers, blacksmiths and laborers when competent people were available.
Article 2: before the United States used the One-day's Hunt tract north of Long Prairie River, the boundary with the Pillager band would be settled to the Pillagers' satisfaction.
Article 4: mixed-blood relatives living with the bands to share in all annuities.

breaches.what: The Commission held the Ojibwe owned the ceded land (Royce Area 268, in central Minnesota between the Crow Wing, Long Prairie and Mississippi rivers) by recognised title, valued it at $600,000 as of April 3, 1848, and held the $80,000 consideration so grossly inadequate as to be unconscionable.
breaches.whoFoundIt: Indian Claims Commission, Minnesota Chippewa Tribe v. United States, Docket 18-T, 25 Ind. Cl. Comm. 157 (1971), as restated in 28 Ind. Cl. Comm. 103 (1972)

source.title: Minnesota Chippewa Tribe v. United States, Docket 18-T, Opinion of the Commission, May 31, 1972
source.publisher: Oklahoma State University Library, Indian Claims Commission Decisions

compensation: Final award of $529,000 (May 31, 1972) in Docket 18-T for the Chippewa of the Mississippi and Lake Superior, being the $600,000 value less $71,000 paid on the claim.
today: The land ceded lies in central Minnesota; the Mississippi bands' descendants are within the Minnesota Chippewa Tribe.

nationVoice.summary: The Band's history says the Mississippi and Pillager Ojibwe made Leech Lake their home from the mid to late 1700s, that the 1847 treaties took the southwest corner of their lands for the Menominee and Winnebago the United States meant to move from Wisconsin, and that the rest was ceded in 1855, when the reservation was set up.

openQuestions: The OCR of the final award is damaged; the $71,000 payment on the claim is read from it and from the $600,000 less $529,000 difference, and should be checked against the printed volume (28 Ind. Cl. Comm. 116).
The land was ceded to make room for the Winnebago (Ho-Chunk) and Menominee removals of 1846 and 1848; that link was not sourced here.
The companion treaty with the Pillager band of August 21, 1847 is queue entry kappler-577 (researched separately).
No tribal account of this treaty was found.

Audit 2026-11-08: the $71,000 credit is stated outright in the 1972 opinion (28 Ind. Cl. Comm. 103), not only derived, so the first open question is settled. The note that no tribal account was found is out of date: nationVoice carries the Leech Lake Band history, which ties the 1847 cessions to the planned Menominee and Winnebago moves from Wisconsin.
